title: Health probe prioritization and eviction strategy for interruptible requests
creator: Priya Agarwal
description: Background: As multi-region capacity pressures occur we must preserve SLOs by making smarter decisions at the probe and admission layer. Current readiness/liveness checks treat all requests equally and our autoscaler responds to noisy probe signals, resulting in oscillation and unnecessary failovers. This ticket designs and implements a prioritized health-probe pipeline and an eviction strategy that favors preservation of high-value (non-interruptible) requests while allowing graceful shedding of low-value/interruptible work. Goals: 1) stabilize autoscaler signals and reduce thrash during regional congestion and partial outages; 2) keep p99 tail latency and error budget burn within SLOs by applying request-aware degradation; 3) integrate the probe prioritization with existing circuit-breaker rules and regional failover policies. This work spans runtime (probe scoring/kvs), admission controller, autoscaler gating, and console observability.
acceptance_criteria: Probe prioritization implemented: readiness/liveness pipeline tags probes with priority score (high/medium/low) based on request attributes and token-weighted heuristic.
Eviction strategy implemented: runtime can mark in-flight requests as interruptible and safely evict or pause lower-priority work under memory/CPU pressure without losing high-priority work.
Autoscaler stability: simulated regional congestion shows a reduction in autoscaler scale-up/scale-down cycles by >= 40% compared to baseline; documented in perf regressions dashboard.

SLO preservation: across chaos tests (node failure, network partition), p99 latency and error-budget burn remain within thresholds for high-priority traffic; console shows clear degradation windows for low-priority traffic only.
Circuit-breaker integration: when circuit triggers, probe pipeline demotes non-essential probes and routes high-priority requests to fallback model variants or regions as configured.
Observability: new dashboards and per-request tags are available in Console to filter by probe-priority, eviction events, and autoscaler decisions.
implementation_notes: Approach: 1) Extend probe payloads with a lightweight priority score calculated at the API gateway using rules defined in a policy table (e.g., auth-tier, customer-contract, request type, token estimate). 2) Runtime will maintain short-term moving averages (5–15s window) per worker for health signals and emit an aggregated priority-aware readiness score to the autoscaler. 3) Admission controller honors 'interruptible' flag and applies an eviction policy that picks candidates by LRU on KV cache residency + request priority. 4) Circuit-breaker hooks will accept a prioritized degradation plan (e.g., demote embeddings jobs, route best-effort reranking to lower-cost quantized variants). Trade-offs: adding priority adds complexity to probe evaluation and increases cross-service contract surface; mitigated by keeping scoring deterministic and policy-driven. Performance: initial micro-benchmarks show priority tagging adds ~0.15ms median overhead on the gateway path; eviction selection is O(log N) for in-flight index and runs asynchronously to avoid request-path blocking.
rollout_plan: Step 1 (canary): deploy probe-priority tagging behind a feature flag in us-west-2 for a subset of tokens (5% of traffic). Monitor probe signal variance and autoscaler cycles.
Step 2 (runtime): enable priority-aware readiness aggregation on dedicated canary runtime nodes and expose metrics. Run synthetic bubble tests to validate eviction correctness.
Step 3 (circuit integration): wire prioritized degradation plan into the regional circuit-breaker policy; run failure injection to confirm fallback behaviors.
Step 4 (observability): publish dashboards, add alerting for unexpected priority-eviction rates and regression on p99 latency for high-priority traffic.
Step 5 (scale): gradually widen coverage to 50% then 100% after 2 stable cycles and postmortem review of canary results.
Rollback: flip feature flags and revert runtime hooks; eviction is designed to be reversible without request loss for non-persistent workloads.
